results.title: Solving Measurement Error with Uncertainty Analysis
results.content: By understanding and mitigating measurement errors through uncertainty analysis, we can enhance the reliability of our measurements, improve the accuracy of our results, and ultimately make more informed and confident decisions based on the data we obtain. This understanding forms the basis for uncertainty analysis, which helps quantify and address measurement errors to ensure accurate and valid results. In conclusion, uncertainty analysis is a fundamental tool in measurement science that helps address measurement errors and improve the accuracy and reliability of results. By quantifying and considering the uncertainties associated with the measurement process, uncertainty analysis provides valuable insights into the limitations and errors in the results. The main steps involved in uncertainty analysis include identifying and categorizing sources of measurement error, propagating uncertainty through mathematical equations or models, and assessing uncertainty and its impact on measurement results. By implementing uncertainty analysis as a routine part of the measurement process, scientists and engineers can minimize the impact of measurement errors and ensure more reliable and trustworthy measurement results.

results.title: Error models and measurement uncertainty – Applications of statistics in Measurement & Testing
results.content: Normally it is not sufficient to divide up a measurement error in a systematic and a random component, but it can also be necessary to describe the error structure with a more complex model. In the interpretation and estimation of measurement errors and uncertainty it can be appropriate to make a division of error according to various partial populations of measurement defined by having one or several of the following factors held constant:. In comparing measurement results, it is important to estimate the distribution of errors under relevant conditions. A useful tool to visualise how different sources of measurement error and uncertainty contribute to the overall measurement result is the Ishikawa diagram also known as a ‘fishbone’ diagram and illustrating a hierarchy of cause and effect. If the measurement error is calculated as a function of other quantities (including corrections for possible influence quantities) then it can be easier to judge the error structure for these (inputs) and thereby derive how the errors propagate to the final result.

results.title: Measurement Error - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: Measurement error is defined as the difference between the true value and the measured value, which arises from imperfections in the measurement method, instrument, or human involvement. It encompasses systematic errors, random errors, and gross errors, each affecting the trueness and precision of measurement results. Measurement error is the difference between the true value and the measured value. In general, the result of a measurement is only an approximation or estimate of the value of the measurand and thus is complete only when accompanied by a statement of the uncertainty of the estimate. The necessary components of any measurement are the method of measurement and the measuring instrument; measurements are often performed with the participation of a person (Rabinovich, 1999). The systematic errors have effects on the trueness of the measuring results. The theory of error is focused only on the study of gross and random errors. Random errors have effects on the precision of the measuring results.

results.title: Measurement error in continuous endpoints in randomised trials: Problems and solutions - Nab - 2019 - Statistics in Medicine - Wiley Online Library
results.content: The finite sample performance of the measurement error corrected estimators of the treatment effect was studied by simulation. In systematic measurement error scenarios, confidence intervals for the corrected estimator for *α*=0.05 were constructed by using the Zero-variance method, the Delta method, the Fieller method, and the Bootstrap method based on 999 replicates (as defined in Section 4.1). In the case of differential measurement error, confidence intervals for the corrected estimator for *α*=0.05 were constructed by using the Zero-Variance method, the Delta method, and the Bootstrap method based on 999 replicates (as defined in Section 4.2). We studied performance of the corrected treatment effect estimators in terms of percentage bias,25 empirical standard error (EmpSE), and square root of the mean squared error (SqrtMSE).26 The performance of the methods for constructing the confidence intervals was studied in terms of coverage and Type-II error.26. Percentage bias, empirical standard error (EmpSE), square root of mean squared error (SqrtMSE), coverage, and average width of CIs of the naive estimator and the corrected estimator for systematic measurement error (*θ*0=0 and *θ*1=1.05 or *θ*1=1.25) for different values of R-squared and different sample sizes of the calibration data set. Percentage bias, empirical standard error (EmpSE), mean squared error (MSE), square root of mean squared error (SqrtMSE), coverage, and average width of CIs of the corrected estimator for differential measurement error (*θ*00=0, *θ*10=1, *θ*01=0, *θ*11=1.05) for different values of R-squared and different sample sizes of the calibration data set. Our study showed that, when measurement error is ignored, not only can trial results be hampered by a loss in precision of the treatment effect estimate (ie, increased Type-II error for a given sample size), but trial inferences can be impacted through bias in the treatment effect estimator and a null hypothesis significance test for the treatment effect can deviate substantially from the nominal level. Our simulation study shows that the effectiveness of correction methods to adjust the trial results for endpoint measurement error are dependent on the size of the calibration sample and the strength of the correlation between the error-free and error-prone measurement of the trial endpoint.
